detail.abstract: Online reviews help consumers evaluate products they cannot physically inspect before purchase. Sensory language, i.e., words engaging the five senses (sound, touch, vision, smell, and taste), can provide valuable information about otherwise inaccessible product experiences and thus can be expected to make reviews more helpful. However, we show that this view is incomplete: the effect of sensory language is both sense-specific and contingent on the textual, visual, and prior-review context. Drawing on the accessibility-diagnosticity framework and analyzing approximately 15 million Amazon reviews, we find that sensory language increases helpful votes, especially in reviews with a stronger first-person perspective and more positive valence. However, the impact of sensory language on helpful votes weakens when prior reviews already provide more sensory information and even turns negative when the review includes images (which compete with review text). Among the senses, using sound words is considered especially helpful. Based on these findings, we recommend that platforms prioritize sensory-rich reviews when they convey personal or positive product experiences and when comparable sensory information is otherwise scarce. Review images are found to function like a doubleedged sword: while they lift helpful votes by themselves, they strongly diminish the effect of sensory language on review helpfulness.

Second, the same process panels are replayed through the full synthetic Contracts A, B, and C, which add consistency, minimum days, daily loss, trailing drawdown, buffers, and payout caps.

The full experiment is repeated independently rather than treating one set of 20,000 paths as the sampling universe. A 20-replication pilot is followed by 250 outer replications, each of which regenerates shocks, repeats panel normalization, applies all six trader types and replays the static barrier and Contracts A-C. The predeclared 95% precision thresholds are met, so the contingent extension to 500 replications is not activated.

The process differences from Gaussian range from -0.867 percentage points for GARCH(1,1) to +0.526 points for positive step-level autocorrelation. Their complete-procedure 95% intervals exclude zero. Rule bundles also produce material differences. For the modeled entrant population, mean Gaussian first-payout probabilities are 6.537% under A, 3.760% under B and 0.568% under C. Under a negative-jump mixture they become 7.286%, 4.046% and 0.688%; under a two-state volatility regime they fall to 5.606%, 3.365% and 0.400%. These intervals measure Monte Carlo uncertainty in the declared synthetic procedure. They do not measure uncertainty about the true market process or a population of real traders.

Matching one-session mean and variance is therefore insufficient to preserve selection, rule interaction, or payout probability. Brownian results remain a transparent benchmark, not a distribution-free forecast.

The extended analysis crosses six processes, six trader types and four monitoring grids and reports seven outputs for every combination, producing 1,008 additional cells. This separates process robustness from the observation rule used to enforce the barrier.

Lim (2026a, 2026b) and Tomàs Fernández (2026) provide contemporary Brownian and first-passage valuation benchmarks for trading-evaluation contracts. detail.abstract: Banks and non-bank lenders have learnt to demonstrate that they know their customers. They now deploy AI agents, built in-house or operated by vendors and partners, that answer customers, triage alerts, recommend and take credit decisions and move money in their name. Regulators have begun to expect agents to be inventoried, identified and traceable to their permissions, but none yet sets a standard for evidencing what each one does. Existing duties on the risk assessment of new technology, internal control, outsourcing and reliance, record keeping, consumer outcomes and senior-manager accountability already require an institution to know what such agents do and may do and to be able to show it. That responsibility does not pass to a vendor. This paper asks how that knowledge can be evidenced when behaviour is stochastic. It borrows the evidentiary architecture of know-your-customer (KYC) and know-your-business (KYB) checks (risk assessment before launch, a file per relationship, risk rating, monitoring with event-driven review, quality assurance, records, independent testing, rules for reliance, attestation) and restates each element for a versioned agent, as a statistical claim with stated confidence wherever it concerns behaviour. Ten criteria cover identity and envelope, the rate of out-of-policy actions, quality assurance, never-observed behaviour, decision consistency, change, records, validation and third-party reliance; a sufficient file yields a revocable Agent Knowledge Statement issued as a W3C Verifiable Credential. We show that the evidence needed grows in proportion to the loss one action can cause, that narrowing an envelope that fails closed preserves evidence, and that a simple hold-out bound on never-observed behaviour is exact. In a synthetic institution of 96 agents with known ground truth, no statement was issued for an agent outside tolerance; 11 files were sufficient as configured and 56 after narrowing each envelope to the autonomy its evidence supports, at a median added human workload of 13% of episodes. Without monitoring, a fourfold rise in errors on day 45 of a quarter left 93% of statements false; with monitoring and look-back, 0.3%, because the evidence was re-based or, in most windows, the statement withheld. A deployable tool runs the framework on an institution's own records, and worked examples at a UK non-bank lender, a UK bank and a US bank show it at work. Python code, tests and an executed notebook accompany the paper.
